content: Certain medical conditions and risk factors should be carefully considered when prescribing oral contraceptives (OCPs). For example, jaundice associated with prior oral contraceptive use, a family history of breast cancer or deep vein thrombosis (DVT)/pulmonary embolism (PE), current or past depression, endometriosis, diabetes mellitus (DM), hypertension (HTN), changes in bone mineral density, renal or hepatic impairment, bone metabolic disease, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), and conditions exacerbated by fluid retention (e.g., migraines, asthma, epilepsy) are all relevant considerations. Acitretin, a medication, can reduce the contraceptive efficacy of norethindrone-based preparations. Women with a history of depression should be closely monitored, and therapy should be stopped if depression recurs to a serious degree. Additionally, oral contraceptives should be discontinued four weeks before major surgery or prolonged immobilization. Patients on warfarin or other oral anticoagulants may require an increased anticoagulant dose when using oral contraceptives. Long-term use of OCPs (five or more years) has been associated with an increased risk of cervical cancer, although human papillomavirus (HPV) remains the primary risk factor. Similarly, prolonged OCP use may increase the risk of liver cancer. Some studies suggest an association between OCP use and an increased risk of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia in certain populations. Benign hepatic adenomas, though rare in the United States, have also been linked to OCP use. In women with hereditary angioedema, exogenous estrogens may induce or worsen symptoms of angioedema. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends waiting at least three weeks after vaginal delivery or six weeks after cesarean section before initiating combined hormonal contraceptives to reduce the risk of VTE. Women with additional VTE risk factors should avoid combined hormonal contraceptives altogether. Extensive epidemiological studies have shown no increased risk of birth defects in women who used OCPs prior to pregnancy. Furthermore, there is no evidence of teratogenic effects, particularly concerning cardiac anomalies and limb reduction defects, when OCPs are inadvertently taken during early pregnancy. Oral contraceptives should not be used to induce withdrawal bleeding as a test for pregnancy, nor should they be used during pregnancy to treat threatened or habitual abortion. If a patient misses two consecutive periods, pregnancy should be ruled out before continuing OCP use. If the patient has not adhered to the prescribed schedule, pregnancy should be considered after the first missed period, and OCP use should be discontinued if pregnancy is confirmed. Small amounts of oral contraceptive steroids have been detected in the breast milk of nursing mothers, with a few reported adverse effects on infants, including jaundice and breast enlargement. Additionally, OCPs administered during the postpartum period may interfere with lactation by reducing the quantity and quality of breast milk. Nursing mothers should be advised to use alternative forms of contraception until they have completely weaned their child. Ethinyl estradiol (EE) and norethindrone acetate are the active components of many OCPs. EE reduces the release of luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) from the hypothalamus and gonadotropin release from the pituitary, while also increasing DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis in target tissues. Norethindrone acetate, a progestin, inhibits gonadotropin secretion, prevents follicular maturation and ovulation, and stimulates mammary tissue growth. EE reaches peak plasma levels approximately eight hours after administration, while norethindrone peaks within one to two hours. Both components are metabolized in the liver, with EE undergoing extensive first-pass metabolism. EE metabolites include estriol and estrone, while norethindrone metabolites are primarily inactive sulfate and glucuronide derivatives. The half-life of EE is approximately 19–24 hours. For postpartum women, the CDC guidelines emphasize waiting three to six weeks before initiating combined hormonal contraceptives to minimize VTE risk. Women with additional VTE risk factors should avoid these contraceptives entirely. Finally, while OCPs are generally safe, individual plans and formulary information may vary, and healthcare providers should consult the most current guidelines and recommendations when prescribing these medications.
